adversarialAssessment.singleMechanismProblem: All survivors rely on ONE coincidence: the extremely common given name/surname 'Alexander' happens to also be an NC county. This is the same signal re-counted across three carriers (an artist's first name, a king, a chapter title), not three independent convergent clues.
adversarialAssessment.genericNameProblem: 'Alexander' is among the most common personal names in English. Any book referencing anyone named Alexander, or Alexander the Great, auto-generates this 'wink.' By the prompt's own rule, generic name matches that would fire for dozens of texts do not count as location-specific.
adversarialAssessment.noLocationSemantics: None of the survivors carry meaning pointing to a treasure SITE; they only note a string collision with a county name. Contrast Hiddenite ('Hidden'+'-ite'), which adds genuine concealment semantics. Alexander adds none.
adversarialAssessment.inflationByDuplicationAndSelfReference: Two of the six rows are literal self-references to the place ('Alexander County' x2) and one is a duplicate king row. The headline score (44.0) and '5 distinct entities' are substantially inflated by counting the place naming itself plus duplicates.
adversarialAssessment.neutralAcceptance: A neutral reader would not accept 'a book mentions Alexander the Great and an artist named Alexander' as evidence the treasure is in Alexander County. Only someone already favoring the NC/Alexander hypothesis would.

verdict: Real NC place, but its winks are one generic-name coincidence re-counted plus self-references/duplicates; no location-specific signal. Not a serious rival.
